Databases

Schemas, tables, describe, row previews, read-only queries with paging, and gated writes on databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle)

Docs / Databases

Area
toil db
Env prefix
TOIL_DB_

skills/toil/db.md

One set of commands for every database engine. Each connection says which engine it uses, and the commands work the same way on all of them.

Engineengine valueStatus
SQLitesqliteintegration: automated tests run against the real engine (Node’s built-in node:sqlite)
PostgreSQLpostgresintegration: automated tests run against PostgreSQL 17 (the official postgres:17 image)
MySQL / MariaDBmysqlintegration: automated tests run against MySQL 8.4 and MariaDB 11.8 (the official mysql:8.4 and mariadb:11.8 images)
SQL Serversqlserverintegration: automated tests run against SQL Server 2022 (the official mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-CU27-ubuntu-22.04 image)
Oracleoracleintegration: automated tests run against Oracle Database 23ai Free (the gvenzl/oracle-free:23.26.3-slim-faststart image)

Supported versions: The oldest SQLite version toil supports hasn’t been established. toil uses the SQLite built into Node, so the version is whichever your Node ships. PostgreSQL is tested against 17; the catalog columns toil reads need 11 or later. MySQL is tested against 8.4 and MariaDB against 11.8; the oldest versions toil supports haven’t been established. SQL Server is tested against 2022; the catalog views and OFFSET ... FETCH toil uses need 2012 or later. Azure SQL Database speaks the same protocol but hasn’t been tested. Oracle is tested against 23ai; Thin mode and the dictionary columns toil reads need 12.1 or later. No release older than 23ai has been run.

SQLite connections

There is nothing to install: toil uses the SQLite built into Node.

KeyRequiredMeaning
engineyessqlite
pathyesAbsolute path to an existing database file. toil never creates one.
writesnotrue lets db execute change data on this connection. Off by default.

Environment variables, for the default db connection:

export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=sqlite
export TOIL_DB_PATH=/srv/data/app.db
# Only if this connection may be written to:
export TOIL_DB_WRITES=true

A named connection, defined entirely from the environment (handy in CI):

export TOIL_CONN_SCRATCH_AREA=db
export TOIL_CONN_SCRATCH_ENGINE=sqlite
export TOIL_CONN_SCRATCH_PATH=/tmp/scratch.db
export TOIL_CONN_SCRATCH_WRITES=true

Config file (~/.toil/config.json), with a read-only connection as the default and a writable scratch copy beside it:

{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app": { "area": "db", "engine": "sqlite", "path": "/srv/data/app.db" },
    "scratch": { "area": "db", "engine": "sqlite", "path": "/tmp/scratch.db", "writes": true }
  },
  "defaults": { "db": { "connection": "app" } }
}

On Windows, write the path with forward slashes or escaped backslashes in JSON: "C:/data/app.db".

PostgreSQL connections

toil speaks PostgreSQL’s wire protocol in plain JavaScript (the pg driver, bundled into toil): no libpq, no psql, nothing to install.

KeyRequiredMeaning
engineyespostgres
hostyesServer host name or address
portnoTCP port. Default 5432.
databaseyesThe database to connect to
useryesThe login role
passwordnoThe role’s password. A secret: an env var or the OS credential store, never the config file.
sslnotrue connects over TLS and verifies the server’s certificate against Node’s CAs, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS and the OS certificate store, so a corporate root in the OS store is trusted. Off by default.
writesnotrue lets db execute change data on this connection. Off by default.

Environment variables, for the default db connection:

export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=postgres
export TOIL_DB_HOST=db.imagile.dev
export TOIL_DB_PORT=5432
export TOIL_DB_DATABASE=app
export TOIL_DB_USER=reader
export TOIL_DB_PASSWORD=<the role's password>
export TOIL_DB_SSL=true

Or keep the connection in config and the password in the OS credential store:

{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app-pg": { "area": "db", "engine": "postgres", "host": "db.imagile.dev", "database": "app", "user": "reader", "ssl": true }
  },
  "defaults": { "db": { "connection": "app-pg" } }
}
toil connections login app-pg   # prompts for the password and stores it

A named connection’s password can also come from TOIL_CONN_APP_PG_PASSWORD.

toil ignores the libpq environment (PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGSSLMODE, PGOPTIONS and the rest) and ~/.pgpass: a connection reaches only the host its own settings name, with only its own password.

Connect with an ordinary role that can read what the agent should see, ideally one with only SELECT grants. See the known limit under “Reads are read-only at the engine”.

MySQL and MariaDB connections

One engine, mysql, covers both. toil speaks their wire protocol in plain JavaScript (the mysql2 driver, bundled into toil): no client library, no mysql CLI, nothing to install.

KeyRequiredMeaning
engineyesmysql
hostyesServer host name or address
portnoTCP port. Default 3306.
databaseyesThe database to connect to. It is also the default schema.
useryesThe account
passwordnoThe account’s password. A secret: an env var or the OS credential store, never the config file.
sslnotrue connects over TLS and verifies the server’s certificate and host name against Node’s and the OS’s certificate stores. Off by default.
writesnotrue lets db execute change data on this connection. Off by default.

Environment variables, for the default db connection:

export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=mysql
export TOIL_DB_HOST=db.imagile.dev
export TOIL_DB_PORT=3306
export TOIL_DB_DATABASE=app
export TOIL_DB_USER=reader
export TOIL_DB_PASSWORD=<the account's password>
export TOIL_DB_SSL=true

Or in config, with the password in the OS credential store:

{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app-mysql": { "area": "db", "engine": "mysql", "host": "db.imagile.dev", "database": "app", "user": "reader", "ssl": true }
  },
  "defaults": { "db": { "connection": "app-mysql" } }
}
toil connections login app-mysql   # prompts for the password and stores it

toil reads no option file (my.cnf, ~/.mylogin.cnf) and no MYSQL_* variable. It never sends the password in clear text (an account using mysql_clear_password fails with AUTH), and it never uploads a local file: LOAD DATA LOCAL is off.

Connect with an account that has only SELECT on what the agent should see. See the known limits under “Reads are read-only at the engine”.

SQL Server connections

toil speaks TDS, SQL Server’s wire protocol, in plain JavaScript (the tedious driver, bundled into toil): no ODBC driver, no sqlcmd, nothing to install. It signs in with a SQL Server login (user name and password), which needs the server to allow SQL Server authentication (mixed mode), or, on Windows only, with Windows authentication ("auth": "windows", below).

KeyRequiredMeaning
engineyessqlserver
hostyesServer host name or address
portnoTCP port. Default 1433. A named instance needs its own port here: toil doesn’t ask the SQL Browser service.
databaseyesThe database to connect to
userfor a SQL loginThe SQL Server login; with "auth": "windows", another domain account to sign in as
passwordnoThe login’s password. A secret: an env var or the OS credential store, never the config file.
sslnotrue encrypts the connection with TLS and verifies the server’s certificate against the OS certificate store. Off by default, which sends the login and every result unencrypted, so turn it on unless the network is trusted. There is no setting to trust any certificate: add the server’s certificate, or your organization’s CA, to the OS store instead.
authnosql (a SQL Server login, the default) or windows (Windows authentication, Windows only)
domainnoWith "auth": "windows" and user: the account’s domain
writesnotrue lets db execute change data on this connection. Off by default.

Environment variables, for the default db connection:

export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=sqlserver
export TOIL_DB_HOST=sql.imagile.dev
export TOIL_DB_PORT=1433
export TOIL_DB_DATABASE=app
export TOIL_DB_USER=toil_reader
export TOIL_DB_PASSWORD=<the login's password>
export TOIL_DB_SSL=true

Or keep the connection in config and the password in the OS credential store:

{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app-sql": { "area": "db", "engine": "sqlserver", "host": "sql.imagile.dev", "database": "app", "user": "toil_reader", "ssl": true }
  },
  "defaults": { "db": { "connection": "app-sql" } }
}
toil connections login app-sql   # prompts for the password and stores it

A named connection’s password can also come from TOIL_CONN_APP_SQL_PASSWORD.

Windows authentication (Windows only)

"auth": "windows" signs in as the Windows user running toil, with no password stored anywhere: Windows proves who you are with the Kerberos ticket (or NTLM) it already holds from your logon.

{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app-sql": { "area": "db", "engine": "sqlserver", "host": "sql.imagile.dev", "database": "app", "auth": "windows", "ssl": true }
  }
}

From the environment, for the default db connection, as the current Windows user:

export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=sqlserver
export TOIL_DB_HOST=sql.imagile.dev
export TOIL_DB_DATABASE=app
export TOIL_DB_AUTH=windows

To sign in as a different domain account, add domain and user (TOIL_DB_DOMAIN, TOIL_DB_USER), and store that account’s password with toil connections login app-sql (Windows Credential Manager), or set TOIL_CONN_APP_SQL_PASSWORD.

Platform"auth": "windows"
WindowsSupported
macOS, LinuxRefused before connecting (CONFIG_INVALID); use a SQL Server login

How it works: Node has no way to ask Windows for a sign-in token, so for each connection toil runs one Windows PowerShell (powershell.exe from the Windows folder, -NoProfile -NonInteractive), which asks Windows’ SSPI Negotiate package for tokens for the server’s SPN, MSSQLSvc/<host>:<port>. The script and every token pass over the process’s stdin and stdout, never its command line. Use the server’s fully qualified name in host, the name its SPN is registered under; with any other name Kerberos can’t find the SPN, and Windows falls back to NTLM if the server and domain allow it.

Windows PowerShell must run in Full Language mode. Where an AppLocker or WDAC policy puts it in Constrained Language mode, Add-Type is blocked, and toil says so with AUTH naming the mode instead of failing the login vaguely. Windows PowerShell 5.1’s Add-Type also compiles a small helper with csc.exe into TEMP, so TEMP must be writable.

Windows authentication is untested against a real server: its tests run the helper against Windows’ own SSPI, and a full multi-step handshake completes, but no run against SQL Server on a domain has happened yet, nor one under a Constrained Language Mode policy.

Connect with a read-only login. SQL Server has no read-only transaction, so toil can’t ask the server to refuse writes the way it does for PostgreSQL. It rolls back every read instead (see “Reads are read-only at the engine”), and the login is what makes the server itself refuse a write. A login whose database user is only in db_datareader is enough:

CREATE LOGIN toil_reader WITH PASSWORD = '<a strong password>';
USE app;
CREATE USER toil_reader FOR LOGIN toil_reader;
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER toil_reader;

Use a second connection, with a login that may write and writes: true, for db execute.

Oracle connections

toil speaks Oracle Net in plain JavaScript (the oracledb driver in Thin mode, bundled into toil): no Instant Client, no sqlplus, no native library, nothing to install. toil never switches the driver to Thick mode.

KeyRequiredMeaning
engineyesoracle
hostyesListener host name or IP address. Nothing else: no port, scheme or descriptor.
portnoListener port. Default 1521.
databaseyesThe service name (FREEPDB1, ORCLPDB1). Not a SID, and not a TNS alias.
useryesThe user. Unquoted, it’s read in upper case, as Oracle does; wrap it in double quotes for a case-sensitive one.
passwordnoThe user’s password. A secret: an env var or the OS credential store, never the config file.
sslnotrue connects over TCPS and verifies the server’s certificate, and that its name matches host, against the OS certificate store. Off by default.
writesnotrue lets db execute change data on this connection. Off by default.
export TOIL_DB_ENGINE=oracle
export TOIL_DB_HOST=db.imagile.dev
export TOIL_DB_PORT=1521
export TOIL_DB_DATABASE=ORCLPDB1
export TOIL_DB_USER=reader
export TOIL_DB_PASSWORD=<the user's password>
{
  "version": 2,
  "connections": {
    "app-ora": { "area": "db", "engine": "oracle", "host": "db.imagile.dev", "database": "ORCLPDB1", "user": "reader" }
  },
  "defaults": { "db": { "connection": "app-ora" } }
}
toil connections login app-ora   # prompts for the password and stores it

toil builds the connect descriptor itself from host, port and database, so it reads no tnsnames.ora, sqlnet.ora, TNS_ADMIN or wallet. Thin mode needs the user’s password to have an 11G or 12C verifier; an older one fails with AUTH, saying so.

Connect with a read-only account: a user granted SELECT (or READ) on what the agent should see, and nothing that writes. On Oracle this matters more than on the other engines; see the known limit under “Reads are read-only at the engine”.

Commands

CommandMCP toolReturns
toil db list-schemasdb_list_schemas{ schemas: [{ name }] }. For SQLite, the attached databases (main); for PostgreSQL, the schemas, without pg_* and information_schema; for MySQL, the databases the account can see, without mysql, sys, performance_schema and information_schema; for SQL Server, the schemas, without sys, INFORMATION_SCHEMA, guest and the db_* role schemas; for Oracle, the users the login can see that Oracle doesn’t maintain.
toil db list-tables [--schema <name>]db_list_tables{ schema, tables: [{ name, type }] }, type being table or view
toil db describe-table <table> [--schema <name>]db_describe_table{ schema, name, type, columns, primaryKey, indexes, foreignKeys }
toil db preview-table <table> [--schema] [--limit] [--cursor]db_preview_tableA page of rows: { columns, rows }
toil db query <sql> [--limit] [--cursor]db_queryA page of rows from one read-only statement: { columns, rows }
toil db execute <sql> --allow-writedb_execute{ changes }: rows inserted, updated or deleted

Every command takes --connection <name>. --schema defaults to the engine’s default schema (main for SQLite, public for PostgreSQL, the connection’s database for MySQL, where a schema is a database, dbo for SQL Server, and the user’s own schema for Oracle). PostgreSQL names are case-sensitive as stored: an unquoted CREATE TABLE People is stored as people. MySQL table names are case-sensitive on most Linux servers. Oracle stores an unquoted name in upper case and reports names as stored (PEOPLE, ID); a schema or table you name that doesn’t exist as written is looked up again in upper case, so describe-table people finds PEOPLE. A quoted mixed-case name ("People") must be typed exactly.

Rows come back as arrays in the order of columns, so a join’s two id columns both survive:

{ "columns": [{ "name": "id", "type": "INTEGER" }, { "name": "name", "type": "TEXT" }],
  "rows": [[1, "Ada"], [2, "Grace"]] }

type is the column’s declared type, or null for an expression. Integers too large for JavaScript come back as strings, and binary values as base64.

PostgreSQL names every result column’s type (integer, character varying(100), timestamp with time zone). numeric comes back as a string, so no digits are lost; json and jsonb as JSON; arrays as arrays. Dates, times, timestamps and intervals come back as the text the server sent, never shifted into the local time zone.

MySQL names each result column’s type from the protocol (INT, BIGINT, VARCHAR, DECIMAL, DATETIME), without lengths; describe-table gives the full column type (varchar(100)). DECIMAL comes back as a string; dates, times and timestamps as the text the server sent; JSON as JSON; BLOB, BINARY and BIT as base64. preview-table orders a table by its primary key, so pages stay stable. In describe-table, a foreign key’s NO ACTION and RESTRICT both read as null: InnoDB enforces them the same way, and MariaDB reports an unstated rule as RESTRICT. SQL Server names every result column’s type as you’d write it in DDL (int, varchar(100), nvarchar(max), decimal(10,2), datetime2(7)). bigint comes back as a number when it fits and a string when it doesn’t; bit as true or false; uniqueidentifier as a string; binary as base64. date, time, datetime, datetime2 and smalldatetime come back as the text of the value the server holds, never shifted into a time zone (2026-01-02 03:04:05.123), to the millisecond: digits past that are dropped. datetimeoffset comes back as the instant in UTC (2026-01-02T01:04:05.000Z), without its original offset. decimal, numeric and money come back as JSON numbers, so a value with more than about 15 significant digits loses the rest; CAST it to varchar in the query when every digit matters. preview-table pages in primary-key order, or in the engine’s own order for a table without one.

Oracle names each result column’s type (NUMBER, VARCHAR2, DATE), and describe-table gives the declared form (NUMBER(10,2), VARCHAR2(100)). A NUMBER is a JSON number when that’s exactly its value, and a string otherwise, so no digits are lost. CLOB comes back as text, BLOB and RAW as base64, BOOLEAN as a boolean, and BINARY_DOUBLE’s NaN and infinities as strings. Dates and timestamps come back exactly as stored, in the shape PostgreSQL and MySQL use, never through the local time zone of the machine running toil: DATE as 2026-01-02 03:04:05, TIMESTAMP with every fractional digit it holds (2026-01-02 03:04:05.123456), and TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE with its offset (2026-01-02 03:04:05+02, +05:30). A value stored with a named region (Europe/Paris) and TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE come back as the same instant in UTC (+00).

Paging and row caps

preview-table and query return 100 rows per page unless you pass --limit (1 to 1000). When there are more, meta.page.nextCursor holds a cursor; pass it back with --cursor, along with the same SQL or table, to get the next page. A cursor only works with the query it came from. Use ORDER BY in a query you page through, so the pages are stable.

Reads are read-only at the engine

db query, preview-table and the listing commands open SQLite read-only with PRAGMA query_only on. A statement that tries to write fails with WRITE_DISABLED, whatever the connection’s writes setting. db query runs exactly one statement; SQL holding several is refused with INVALID_INPUT.

VACUUM is refused on every read with INVALID_INPUT, before it reaches SQLite. VACUUM INTO '<file>' creates its target file even on a read-only connection, so reads never get the chance. To vacuum or to write a copy, use db execute with writes on; it runs a lone VACUUM outside the usual transaction, because SQLite can’t vacuum inside one, and refuses VACUUM mixed with other statements.

One known gap remains: ATTACH DATABASE from a read-only query can open another existing SQLite file for reading (it can’t create one). If the files a connection can reach matter, run toil as a user that can read only what it should.

PostgreSQL runs every read in a transaction begun with SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY and rolled back, on a connection opened for that one call. The server refuses any write (INSERT, UPDATE, DDL, nextval, a data-modifying WITH) with SQLSTATE 25006, which comes back as WRITE_DISABLED. db query sends its statement on the extended protocol, which refuses a second one, so several statements are INVALID_INPUT here too.

COPY and DO are refused on every read with INVALID_INPUT, before they reach the server: COPY ... TO '<file>' writes a file on the server, and TO PROGRAM runs one, even in a read-only transaction, for a role allowed to, and a DO block can run the same COPY. Neither returns rows a query could page. To run them, use db execute.

Known limit: functions with effects outside the database still run in a read-only transaction for a role allowed to call them. lo_export writes a server file, pg_terminate_backend ends sessions, pg_reload_conf reloads the server’s config, and an extension such as dblink can reach another database. They can’t be refused by name, so connect with an ordinary role: not a superuser, and not a member of pg_write_server_files, pg_execute_server_program or pg_signal_backend.

MySQL and MariaDB run every read on a session set to SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY, inside START TRANSACTION READ ONLY, rolled back, on a connection opened for that one call. Both are needed: DDL commits the transaction implicitly, and the session setting makes the server refuse it all the same. Any write (INSERT, UPDATE, DDL, LOAD DATA) fails with error 1792, which comes back as WRITE_DISABLED. db query sends one statement with multi-statements off; several are INVALID_INPUT.

SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE, INTO DUMPFILE and every SET are refused on reads with INVALID_INPUT, before they reach the server: INTO OUTFILE writes a server file even in a read-only transaction, for an account with FILE, and SET GLOBAL or SET PERSIST changes the server’s configuration. To run them, use db execute.

Known limits: a stored procedure that commits and switches its own session to read-write can still write when a read CALLs it, and administrative statements that aren’t writes (KILL, FLUSH, SHUTDOWN) run for an account allowed to. Neither can be refused by name without refusing ordinary reads, so connect with an account that has SELECT only: no FILE, SUPER, SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN or CONNECTION_ADMIN, and no EXECUTE on procedures that change data. SQL Server has no read-only transaction. toil runs every read in a transaction, on a connection opened for that one call, and always rolls it back, so nothing a read does is kept. The server reports the type of every statement it runs, and a read whose statement the server reports as changing data or schema (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, SELECT INTO, CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, UPDATE STATISTICS, including inside EXEC) comes back as WRITE_DISABLED. With a read-only login the server refuses the write itself, which comes back as WRITE_DISABLED too. db query returns one result: SQL that returns a second result is INVALID_INPUT. When the first result fills the page, toil stops the batch there with a TDS attention, so anything after it in the same SQL never runs.

COMMIT, ROLLBACK, BEGIN TRANSACTION and SAVE TRANSACTION are refused on every read with INVALID_INPUT, before they reach the server: a COMMIT would end the transaction toil rolls back, and keep the write before it. An OUTPUT clause is refused on reads too: an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE with OUTPUT sends its rows before the server reports the change, so a full page could stop it before toil learns it was a write. A column or alias named output in a plain SELECT is fine; in SQL that also holds one of those words, bracket-quote it as [output]. A read-only login’s refusal of a permission that only reads (a sys.dm_db_* view needing VIEW DATABASE STATE, SHOWPLAN) comes back as DATABASE, naming the permission.

Known limit: transaction control inside dynamic SQL or a procedure (an EXEC whose text holds a COMMIT) can’t be refused by name, and neither can an OUTPUT clause there (EXEC('UPDATE ... OUTPUT ...')): its changed rows can fill a page and come back as an ordinary result, though the change is still rolled back. A write under SET NOCOUNT ON isn’t reported by the server. toil notices the transaction ending and says so with DATABASE (“anything it changed may have been saved”), but by then the change is made. That is why a SQL Server connection for reads should use a read-only login: with one, the server refuses the write whatever the SQL does.

Oracle runs every read in a transaction begun with SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY and rolled back, on a connection opened for that one call. The server refuses INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with ORA-01456, which comes back as WRITE_DISABLED, as do a read-only user or session (ORA-28193) and a database open read-only (ORA-16000). db query runs one statement; several are INVALID_INPUT.

That transaction doesn’t hold everything, so some statements are refused on every read before they reach the server:

  • DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, GRANT, REVOKE, COMMENT, ANALYZE, PURGE, FLASHBACK, NOAUDIT, ASSOCIATE, DISASSOCIATE) is WRITE_DISABLED: Oracle commits before and after DDL, so it runs, and stays, inside a read-only transaction.
  • PL/SQL (BEGIN, DECLARE, CALL, and WITH FUNCTION or WITH PROCEDURE) is INVALID_INPUT: a block can COMMIT, EXECUTE IMMEDIATE DDL, or run an autonomous transaction, and CALL reaches built-ins such as DBMS_UTILITY.EXEC_DDL_STATEMENT.

To run any of them, use db execute.

Known limit: a stored function that runs an autonomous transaction (PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION) still writes when a SELECT calls it, and a function can’t be refused by name. Connect with an account that can’t write: then nothing a query calls can either. AUDIT isn’t refused either: it needs the audit privileges an ordinary account doesn’t have. A trigger or stored function with an autonomous transaction commits on its own; toil can’t see it, so “nothing was applied” after a failed db execute covers only the script’s own transaction.

Writes

db execute is the only command that changes data. It needs both:

  1. writes: true on the connection (TOIL_DB_WRITES=true, or TOIL_CONN_<NAME>_WRITES=true), set by the person who owns the config, and
  2. --allow-write on the call (allowWrite: true over MCP).

Without either it fails with WRITE_DISABLED and changes nothing. It runs one or more statements, separated by semicolons, in one transaction that commits only if every statement succeeds. A script that starts or ends a transaction of its own (BEGIN, COMMIT, END, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, RELEASE, and for PostgreSQL also START, ABORT and PREPARE TRANSACTION; for MySQL also START TRANSACTION, XA, LOCK and UNLOCK TABLES, and SET autocommit) is refused with INVALID_INPUT before any of it runs.

On MySQL and MariaDB, DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE) commits implicitly, so a script holding DDL isn’t all or nothing: what ran before the DDL is committed even if a later statement fails. Keep DDL in a script of its own. A server running read_only, or an account whose transactions default to read-only, fails writes with DATABASE, saying so. On SQL Server that means BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVE TRANSACTION; BEGIN ... END blocks, TRY ... CATCH and CASE are fine. A SQL Server script runs as one batch, so leave out GO, and a statement that must start a batch (CREATE VIEW, CREATE PROCEDURE) goes in a call of its own. changes counts the rows INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE and SELECT INTO reported; under SET NOCOUNT ON the server reports none.

On PostgreSQL, statements that can’t run inside a transaction (VACUUM, CREATE DATABASE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) fail with DATABASE; run those with your own tools. A connection that reaches a read-only standby, or a role whose transactions default to read-only, fails writes with DATABASE, saying so.

On Oracle, a script’s statements are separated by semicolons, and a PL/SQL unit (a BEGIN or DECLARE block, CREATE FUNCTION, PROCEDURE, PACKAGE, TRIGGER or TYPE) runs to a line holding only /, as in SQL*Plus, or to the end of the script. COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT and SET TRANSACTION are refused before any of it runs. Two things Oracle does break all-or-nothing, and toil can’t stop them: DDL commits everything before it, and itself, as it runs, and a PL/SQL block can commit inside. When a script fails after Oracle has committed part of it (a DDL statement that ran, or failed after parsing), the error says which statements stayed committed (Oracle committed statements 1 to 2 of 4). After a PL/SQL block or a CALL ran, toil can’t see whether it committed, so the error says the statements up to the failure may have committed; check before running the script again. Only when nothing in the script could have committed does it say nothing was applied (an autonomous-transaction trigger or function is the exception; see the known limit above). Keep DDL in a script of its own, or first.

Time limits and cancelling

Every command stops at TOIL_TIMEOUT_MS (default 120000) with TIMEOUT, and on Ctrl+C or an MCP cancel with CANCELLED. The answer comes back straight away. SQLite can only be stopped between rows, though: a statement that computes for a long time before producing its first row keeps running in the background until it finishes, and the CLI process exits only then. Prefer LIMIT and indexed filters on large tables.

PostgreSQL stops the statement on the server: on a time limit or a cancel, toil asks the server to cancel it (pg_cancel_backend, from a second short connection), so a long sort or pg_sleep doesn’t keep running after toil has answered. db query reads rows a batch at a time from a server-side portal, so the server stops producing rows once the page is full.

MySQL stops the statement on the server too, with KILL <id> from a second short connection. That ends the whole session, so a cancelled db execute rolls back and runs none of its remaining statements. Its protocol has no portal, so db query reads rows as they stream and, once the page is full, drops the connection; the server stops at the next row it tries to send. SQL Server stops the statement on the server too: on a time limit or a cancel, toil sends a TDS attention, which ends the running batch, and the read’s transaction is rolled back when its connection closes.

Oracle is sent a break (connection.break()) on a time limit or a cancel, which stops the statement on the server at its next check: a long join or sort stops at once. Thin mode’s break travels in the data stream, so a session parked in DBMS_SESSION.SLEEP hears it only when the sleep ends; toil still answers straight away. db query reads rows a batch at a time from a server-side cursor.

Examples

toil db list-tables
toil db describe-table people
toil db preview-table people --limit 20
toil db query "SELECT id, name FROM people WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY id" --limit 50
toil db query "SELECT id, name FROM people WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY id" --limit 50 --cursor <meta.page.nextCursor>
toil db execute "UPDATE people SET active = 0 WHERE id = 7" --allow-write --connection scratch

Over MCP:

{ "name": "db_query", "arguments": { "sql": "SELECT id, name FROM people ORDER BY id", "limit": 50 } }

Errors

CodeMeans
NOT_CONFIGUREDNo db connection set up
CONFIG_INVALIDA connection is missing engine or a key its engine needs (path; host, database, user), path is relative, the file isn’t a SQLite database, "auth": "windows" is set off Windows, or an Oracle host or database holds more than a host name or service name
AUTHThe server refused the login: check user and password (for SQL Server, also that SQL Server logins are allowed; for Oracle, also a locked or expired account, or a password verifier too old for Thin mode); or Windows authentication couldn’t start (Constrained Language mode, SSPI refused)
NETWORKThe server or listener couldn’t be reached, didn’t answer, or its TLS certificate wasn’t trusted; or SQL Server requires encryption and ssl is off
NOT_FOUNDThe file, database, Oracle service, schema or table doesn’t exist
WRITE_DISABLEDA write was refused: by db query (DDL included, on Oracle), or by the write gate on db execute
INVALID_INPUTBad flags, a cursor from another query, several statements in db query, or on a read VACUUM (SQLite), COPY and DO (PostgreSQL), INTO OUTFILE and SET (MySQL), transaction control and OUTPUT (SQL Server), or PL/SQL (Oracle)
DATABASEThe engine refused or failed the statement: bad SQL, a constraint, a lock, a permission; on SQL Server, also SQL that ended toil’s transaction itself
TIMEOUT, CANCELLEDStopped waiting; for db execute, check whether the change was made before retrying

Commands at a glance

  • toil dblist-schemas

    List the schemas in a database

    MCP db_list_schemas

  • toil dblist-tables

    List the tables and views in a schema

    MCP db_list_tables--schema <name>

  • toil dbdescribe-table

    Describe a table or view: columns, primary key, indexes and foreign keys

    MCP db_describe_table<table>--schema <name>

  • toil dbpreview-table

    Preview the rows of a table or view, a page at a time

    MCP db_preview_table<table>--schema <name>--limit <rows>--cursor <cursor>

  • toil dbquery

    Run one read-only SQL statement and return a page of its rows

    MCP db_query<sql>--limit <rows>--cursor <cursor>

  • toil dbexecutewrite

    Run SQL that changes data, in one transaction (needs writes on and --allow-write)

    MCP db_execute<sql>--allow-write
